findings.text: Xen console state keeps membership linkage for a global collection together with the owning bus device, a pointer to a shared area, event channel and interrupt identity, a terminal number, a grant handle, an HVC association, output progress tracking with a staleness counter, and a private guard for index updates.
The distinguished terminal number for the primary Xen console equals hex 58656e, mnemonic for Xen.

A global spin guard serializes membership operations on the Xen console collection, including lookup by terminal number, insertion during initialization and probe, and removal during teardown. Lookups hold the guard across traversal and return the matching entry without retaining the guard, so callers must tolerate later removal.

Each console instance has its own ring guard that serializes access to shared producer and consumer positions for both directions, including validation of index distance, copying between the ring and caller buffers, updating the owned position, and sampling backend progress for spurious detection.

Secondary Xenbus console terminal numbers derive deterministically by adding the Xenbus device identifier to the primary base value. Device zero is rejected during probe, so only positive identifiers yield usable secondary numbers.

Both transmit and receive paths validate that producer minus consumer distance does not exceed the corresponding ring capacity before touching ring storage. On violation they release guards, emit a one-time diagnostic, and fail the operation rather than copying.

Guest transmit first resolves the terminal number to an instance and rejects unknown instances and disconnected backends. It then repeatedly offers the remaining caller bytes to the shared output area, notifies the backend when progress occurs, and yields the processor while incomplete, returning only after the whole caller length is accepted or on error.

Guest receive resolves the terminal number, validates input index distance, drains available input bytes up to the caller length, publishes the consumed position, and notifies the backend when data was taken. It tracks backend output consumption across calls and flags the late interrupt completion as spurious only after consecutive empty rounds with no newly consumed output.

Frontend handling of backend state changes ignores intermediate and unknown states, acknowledges the connected state by moving the frontend to connected, and on closing or closed states removes the HVC association if present before marking the frontend closed, while avoiding duplicate closed transitions.

Secondary console bring-up allocates and zeroes state, assigns the derived terminal number and a fresh page for the shared area, allocates a channel and binds a late interrupt, creates the HVC association with output quota 256, claims and grants the page to the peer, publishes ring and port attributes transactionally with retry on contention, then announces initialization and joins the global set. Teardown removes the HVC association, releases interrupt and channel resources, frees grant references, unlinks from the set, and frees memory, with resume performing teardown of transport only, clearing the shared page, and repeating connection. The bus driver matches the console identifier and wires probe, remove, resume and peer-change handlers under the xenconsole name.

PowerPC VIO hypervisor console discovers the boot terminal from firmware stdout when its name indicates a virtual terminal, reads its unit number, prepares per-terminal state and its buffer guard, selects raw or handshake protocol by compatibility, wires low-level debug input and output, performs handshake for the handshake variant, requests the HVC preferred console unless the command line already names one, and instantiates terminal zero. Debug entry variants skip registration when running with hypervisor privilege, otherwise install terminal zero with fixed numbering and debug operations, including handshake setup for the handshake variant. Normal probe allocates per-terminal state for non-boot units, initializes its guard and handshake library as needed, creates the HVC instance with a bounded output size, records driver data, and installs debug operations for index zero when absent, with the bus driver registered at init time and bound by table to probe under its driver name while suppressing bind attributes.

Xen HVC selects between direct hypercall operations and shared-ring operations based on a boolean that defaults to initial-domain status but can be forced via a kernel option parsed as boolean. Early setup instantiates the primary terminal with the chosen operations after preparing HVM or PV shared state. Late setup prepares the same shared state for non-initial domains or binds a virtual interrupt for initial domains, binds the event channel to a late interrupt when using rings, disables probing on the resulting interrupt, creates the primary HVC instance with output quota 256, and registers the frontend bus driver when configured, cleaning up membership and transport on allocation failure. HVM preparation reads channel and frame parameters, rejects zero values indicating an unprepared toolstack, and maps the frame, while PV preparation uses start information channel and frame and rejects missing channels.

Externally visible helpers include resume handling that refreshes the event channel from current parameters unless direct hypercall mode is active and then rebinds the interrupt, plus raw output that first attempts a hypercall write and falls back to a legacy port write on HVM when the hypercall is unavailable, with a formatted wrapper using a fixed temporary buffer.

Boot consoles exposed consist of a named xenboot console with print-buffer, boot and anytime flags and unassigned index, wired to setup and write handlers, plus an early console setup that installs a direct hypercall write handler.

Xen boot output first tries direct hypercall emission and succeeds without further work when supported. Otherwise on non-paravirtualized guests it uses legacy port emission, while on paravirtualized guests it prefixes an early marker and expands each newline into carriage return plus newline while streaming via shared-ring transmit, after initializing shared state from start information during setup for non-initial paravirtualized domains.
The HVCS driver reports version one point three point three and defines a close wait equal to one tenth of a second derived from the timer frequency.

HVCS sizing defaults request sixty four server adapters, allow up to one thousand twenty four, start minor numbering at zero, align certain structures to eight bytes, use a sixteen byte internal buffer, and cap single user transfers at four thousand ninety six bytes.

Default terminal settings ignore break and parity on input, enable post-processing on output, and request thirty eight thousand four hundred baud with eight data bits plus read enable and hangup on close, with standard control characters. Driver globals hold a configurable device count defaulting to negative one, fixed driver and node names, rescan status, a tty driver pointer, a dynamic index list with its count, and a kicked flag.

Failure modes include illegal ring indices that abort input or output, disconnected backends that reject transmit, unknown terminal numbers that fail both directions, missing firmware properties or unsupported protocols that abort early VIO setup, allocation failures that unwind probe state, and unprepared HVM parameters that reject console bring-up.
